title: - “Wonderful, Venerable Kaccāna! Marvelous, Venerable Kaccāna! The way Venerable Kaccāna has defined non-guarding of the sense faculties is excellent. Venerable Kaccāna has spoken of…
content: - “Wonderful, Venerable Kaccāna! Marvelous, Venerable Kaccāna! The way Venerable Kaccāna has defined non-guarding of the sense faculties is excellent. Venerable Kaccāna has spoken of ‘guarding of the sense faculties, guarding of the sense faculties.’ To what extent, Venerable Kaccāna, is there guarding of the sense faculties?” - “Here, brahmin, a monk, when seeing a form with the eye, his mind does not incline toward agreeable forms nor recoil from disagreeable forms. He dwells with mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Therefore, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. When he hears a sound … smells an odor … tastes a flavor … feels a touch … cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, his mind does not incline toward agreeable phenomena nor recoil from disagreeable phenomena. He dwells with mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Therefore, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. Thus, brahmin, is the guarding of the sense faculties.”

title: Behold this decorated image — A heap of wounds, a collection of sores, Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts, Nothing stable or permanent here.…
content:
Behold this decorated image —
A heap of wounds, a collection of sores,
Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts,
Nothing stable or permanent here.

Behold this adorned appearance,
With jewels and earrings,
A skeleton covered by skin,
Made beautiful by clothes.

The feet are painted with lac and dye,
The face is smeared with powder and paste —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

The hair is curled in seven rings,
The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

title: “Being infatuated by craving, brahmin, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one plans for one’s own harm, plans for others’ harm, plans for the harm of both,…
content: “Being infatuated by craving, brahmin, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one plans for one’s own harm, plans for others’ harm, plans for the harm of both, and experiences mental suffering and mental distress. When craving is abandoned, one does not plan for one’s own harm, nor for others’ harm, nor for the harm of both, and does not experience mental suffering or mental distress. Thus, brahmin, the Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise.”

title: “One without craving, wise, Without doubt, Having merged into the deathless — Him I call a brahmin.” “One who in this world Is not stained…
content:
“One without craving, wise,
Without doubt,
Having merged into the deathless —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“One who in this world
Is not stained by good and evil,
Griefless, stainless, pure —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Like the moon, stainless,
Clear, pure, calm,
With craving for existence destroyed —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Who has crossed this dangerous path,
Saṃsāra and delusion,
Gone to the further shore,
Meditative, without sensual desire, without doubt,
Not clinging, at peace —
Him I call a brahmin.”

title: Elder Talapuṭa: O mind, everywhere, I have acted as you wished, For many lives — You were not angry with me, And this inner-born body…
content:
Elder Talapuṭa:

O mind, everywhere,
I have acted as you wished,
For many lives —
You were not angry with me,
And this inner-born body
Is your gratitude!
On the long path of saṃsāra,
Suffering was caused by you.

O mind, you yourself made
This person that I am —
You made me become
A brahmin,
A king, a royal,
One day a merchant,
Another day a servant,
Or a kind of deity —
All is due to you,
Made by you.

Due to your power,
We became asuras —
Due to you,
I fell to the bottom of hell;
Sometimes an animal,
Sometimes a hungry ghost —
All is due to you,
Made by you.

You will not deceive me
Again, many times more,
Like sorcerers
Performing magic tricks.
You played tricks on me,
Like playing with a madman.
O mind, tell me —
Where have I wronged you?

Formerly this mind wandered,
Went wherever it wished,
Went where it delighted,
Went where it enjoyed —
Now I will restrain it
With wise reflection,
As with a hook one restrains
A rutting elephant.

For me, the Teacher
Has declared that life is impermanent —
Life is not eternal,
Life has no core.
O mind, urge me
To leap into the Buddha’s teaching —
Make me cross the flood,
So very hard to cross.

I have now gone forth
In the Great Sage’s Dhamma —
Those like me
Do not accept loss.

Forests, oceans, rivers, land,
The four directions, above and below —
All are impermanent.
The three realms are perilous.
O mind, where will you go?
You will enjoy peace.

title: “O brahmin, strive to cut the stream, Abandon sensual pleasures. Knowing the destruction of formations, You will be the one who knows the Unmade.” “By…
content:
“O brahmin, strive to cut the stream,
Abandon sensual pleasures.
Knowing the destruction of formations,
You will be the one who knows the Unmade.”

“By always dwelling in two Dhammas,
One reaches the further shore.
That brahmin, wise,
Cuts off all fetters.”

“One who has no near shore, no far shore,
No both shores,
Free from suffering, unbound —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Meditating, free from dust,
Duty done, without defilements,
Having attained the highest goal —
Him I call a brahmin.”

title: “Rādha, whatever is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Rādha, is suffering? The eye, Rādha, is suffering — there you should…
content: “Rādha, whatever is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Rādha, is suffering? The eye, Rādha, is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Forms … Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact … that feeling is suffering. There you should abandon your desire. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind … Phenomena … Mind-consciousness … Mind-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact … that feeling is suffering. There you should abandon your desire. Whatever is suffering, Rādha — there you should abandon your desire.”

title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied, infatuated, or utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who see their peril, who…
content: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied, infatuated, or utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who see their peril, who know the escape from them, and who enjoy them—they should be understood as not fallen into misfortune, not fallen into calamity, and are not being used by Māra as he wishes. Monks, just as a forest deer that has not fallen into a trap does not have to lie down—that deer should be understood as not fallen into misfortune, not fallen into calamity, and is not being used by the hunter as he wishes. When the hunter comes, the deer can leave as it wishes. So too, monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are not tied … are not being used by Māra as he wishes.”

title: “Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling, monks, should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should…
content:
“Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling, monks, should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should be seen as a dart. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent. When, monks, a monk sees pleasant feeling as suffering, sees painful feeling as a dart, sees neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent — then, monks, he is called a monk who has right view, who has cut off craving, who has destroyed the fetters. By thoroughly breaking through conceit, he has made an end of suffering.

One who sees pleasure as suffering,
And sees pain as a dart,
Sees the neutral feeling
As impermanent —
That monk sees rightly,
Fully understanding feelings.

Having fully understood feelings,
He is defilement-free in this very life.
At the breaking of the body, that Dhamma-abider,
The great sage, is beyond measure.”

title: “Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with…
content:
“Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … with feeling … with perception … with formations … with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’

Happy indeed are the arahants,
In them no craving is found,
Conceit has been cut off,
The net of delusion is torn apart.

They have attained the imperturbable,
Their minds are far from defilement,
They are not stained in the world —
The holy ones, free from defilements.

Fully understanding the five aggregates,
Practicing the seven good qualities,
Praised by true persons,
Disciples of the Buddha.

Possessing seven treasures,
Completed in the three trainings,
The great heroes wander forth,
Having abandoned all fear.

Endowed with ten powers,
The great elephant is concentrated,
They are supreme in the world,
Craving has been destroyed.

Achieved the knowledge of the adept,
This body is their last,
The end of the holy life,
Achieved independently.

Not shaken by perceptions,
Liberated from renewed existence,
Having reached the tamed state,
They are conquerors in the world.

Above, below, and across,
They have no delight,
They roar the lion’s roar —
The supreme Buddhas in the world!
